```{r}
#| label: setup-display
#| include: false

# Display-only render by default: reads saved CSV/PNG artifacts.

run_analysis <- FALSE

suppressPackageStartupMessages({

  library(glue)
  library(knitr)
  library(DT)
})

wkdir <- "/resnick/groups/mthomson/jboktor/WILDRxSPF_brains"
run_tag <- "2026-10-04"                  # current popAlign run; 2026-10-02 run superseded (see Code & Provenance)
synth_tag <- "2026-10-05"                # current synthesis of that run (Ensembl GO + contamination flag)
pa_base <- file.path(wkdir, "data/interim/popalign/snRNASeq")
fig_dir <- file.path(wkdir, "figures/popAlign/snRNASeq", glue("run_{run_tag}_synth-{synth_tag}"))
tbl_dir <- file.path(wkdir, "tables/popAlign/snRNASeq", glue("run_{run_tag}_synth-{synth_tag}"))
log_dir <- file.path(wkdir, ".cluster_runs/popalign")

manifest_f <- file.path(pa_base, glue("manifest_{run_tag}.csv"))
manifest <- if (file.exists(manifest_f)) read_csv(manifest_f, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()
read_tbl <- function(name) { f <- file.path(tbl_dir, name); if (file.exists(f)) read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL }
unit_status <- read_tbl("popAlign_unit_status.csv")
catalog <- read_tbl("popAlign_subpopulation_catalog.csv")
has_results <- !is.null(catalog)
lv_order <- c("class", "subclass", "supertype")

n_units <- nrow(manifest)
n_by_level <- if (n_units) table(factor(manifest$level, lv_order)) else c(class = 0, subclass = 0, supertype = 0)
n_done <- if (is.null(unit_status)) 0L else sum(unit_status$status == "ok")
n_substructure <- if (is.null(unit_status)) NA else sum(unit_status$atlas_K > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_robust <- if (has_results) sum(catalog$robust & !catalog$contamination_flag, na.rm = TRUE) else NA
n_shift <- if (has_results) sum(catalog$microbiome_effect %in% c("abundance", "state", "abundance + state")) else NA

leads <- read_tbl("popAlign_followup_leads.csv")          # build_popalign_report_assets_sn.R
mp_sum <- read_tbl("popAlign_meta_program_summary.csv")
abund_t <- read_tbl("popAlign_abundance_tests.csv")
omni_t <- read_tbl("popAlign_abundance_omnibus.csv")
state_t <- read_tbl("popAlign_state_shift_tests.csv")
xmap <- read_tbl("popAlign_cross_level_map.csv")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(round(100 * x, d), "%")
if (has_results) {
  rc <- catalog %>% filter(robust, !contamination_flag)
  k_med <- unit_status %>% group_by(level) %>% summarise(m = median(atlas_K)) %>% deframe()
  k1 <- unit_status %>% group_by(level) %>% summarise(n = sum(atlas_K == 1)) %>% deframe()
  kagree <- unit_status %>% group_by(level) %>% summarise(m = median(boot_K_agreement)) %>% deframe()
  ab_nr <- abund_t %>% filter(!redundant)
  # tests with too few animals have NA p: count only tests that were actually run
  ab_nr <- ab_nr %>% filter(!is.na(p_perm)); omni_t <- omni_t %>% filter(!is.na(p_omnibus))
  state_t <- state_t %>% filter(!is.na(p_perm))
  n_ab <- nrow(ab_nr); n_ab05 <- sum(ab_nr$p_perm < 0.05)
  n_om <- nrow(omni_t); n_om05 <- sum(omni_t$p_omnibus < 0.05); minq_om <- min(omni_t$q_omnibus)
  n_st <- nrow(state_t); n_st05 <- sum(state_t$p_perm < 0.05); minq_st <- min(state_t$q_perm)
  n_depth <- sum(catalog$depth_flag); n_contam <- sum(catalog$contamination_flag)
  eta <- catalog %>% distinct(unit_id, level, unit_depth_eta2) %>% group_by(level) %>%
    summarise(m = median(unit_depth_eta2)) %>% deframe()
  kinds <- rc %>% count(level, kind) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = kind, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
  xl_share <- xmap %>% group_by(coarse_level, fine_level, coarse_unit, coarse_comp) %>%
    summarise(top = max(p), .groups = "drop") %>% group_by(coarse_level) %>%
    summarise(med = median(top), frac50 = mean(top >= 0.5)) %>% split(.$coarse_level)
}

enr <- read_tbl("popAlign_circuit_enrichment.csv")         # circuit enrichment (report assets)
dvc <- read_tbl("popAlign_deg_vs_composition.csv")         # MAST DEGs vs composition shift
E <- function(scope, field, outcome = "hit") {               # pull one enrichment number
  if (is.null(enr)) return(NA)
  v <- enr[[field]][enr$scope == scope & enr$outcome == outcome & enr$grouping == "circuit"]
  if (length(v)) v[1] else NA
}
ORf <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x); Pf <- function(x) format(signif(x, 2), scientific = FALSE)
if (!is.null(dvc)) {
  dvc_top <- dvc %>% group_by(level) %>% slice_max(n_deg, prop = 0.25, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup()
  deg_rho <- cor.test(log1p(dvc$n_deg), -log10(dvc$p_omnibus), method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
}

# Show a saved figure, or a placeholder if the pipeline has not produced it yet.
show_fig <- function(name) {
  f <- file.path(fig_dir, glue("popAlign_{name}.png"))
  if (file.exists(f)) knitr::include_graphics(f) else
    cat(glue("*Not yet computed — `{basename(f)}` is written by `run_popalign_synthesis_sn.R` (run {run_tag}).*"))
}
fmt <- function(x) if (is.na(x)) "—" else format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

## Overview

**Bottom line.** Across `r n_units` cell-type units at three Allen levels, the microbiome leaves
the *make-up* of cell types intact. It does appear to shift the *expression state* of cells in one
circuit: the medial amygdala → bed nucleus of the stria terminalis → medial hypothalamus network,
which carries chemosensory social signals into neuroendocrine and behavioural output. No single
shift survives FDR with 6 vs 6 animals. The evidence is that sub-threshold shifts concentrate in
this network far more than chance allows.

::: {.stat-row}
::: {.stat}
[`r ORf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "odds_ratio"))`×]{.stat-value}
[Enrichment of state shifts in the MeA–BST–hypothalamus network (p = `r Pf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "p"))`)]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[0 / `r if (has_results) n_om else "—"`]{.stat-value}
[Units whose subpopulation mix changes (FDR)]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[`r fmt(n_robust)`]{.stat-value}
[Robust subpopulations discovered]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[`r fmt(n_units)`]{.stat-value}
[Cell-type units modelled (class / subclass / supertype)]{.stat-label}
:::
:::

### What is interesting

1. **The microbiome signal sits in one circuit.** Units from the medial amygdala, BST and medial
   hypothalamic nuclei carry a microbiome-associated state shift at
   `r sprintf("%.1f", E("all levels", "rate_in") / E("all levels", "rate_out"))`× the rate of all other
   cell types: `r E("all levels", "in_group_hits")` / `r E("all levels", "in_group_units")`
   vs `r E("all levels", "out_group_hits")` / `r E("all levels", "out_group_units")` units (adjusted
   odds ratio `r ORf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "odds_ratio"))`,
   p = `r Pf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "p"))`). They contain
   `r E("all levels", "in_group_hits", "strong")` of the
   `r E("all levels", "in_group_hits", "strong") + E("all levels", "out_group_hits", "strong")`
   strongest shifts. The enrichment holds at subclass and supertype level separately, and is not
   explained by unit size, number of subpopulations, or GABA vs glutamate identity
   ([Fig. A](#sec-circuit)).
2. **It changes how cells are tuned, not how many there are.** No unit changes its subpopulation
   mix (0 / `r if (has_results) n_om else "—"` at FDR; nominal hits run *below* chance). The gene
   programs that move are synaptic (*Erbb4, Htr2c, Nrg1, Gria1, Grm1, Grik1*), with no
   immediate-early activity genes. That suggests durable retuning rather than an acute
   difference in activity.
3. **It reframes the differential-expression results.** The
   `r if (!is.null(dvc)) nrow(dvc_top) else "—"` units with the most MAST DEGs (median
   `r if (!is.null(dvc)) median(dvc_top$n_deg) else "—"` per unit) show no composition change at all
   (smallest p = `r if (!is.null(dvc)) round(min(dvc_top$p_omnibus), 2) else "—"`). Microbiome DEGs
   therefore reflect regulation *within* stable cell populations, not a shifting cell mix
   ([Fig. B](#sec-deg)).
4. **Specific populations to chase.** MEA-BST Lhx6 Nr2e1 GABA (amygdala) and DMH Hmx2 GABA
   (hypothalamus) are each flagged by both the subclass and the supertype model. PVH *Avp* neurons
   and an expanding MEA-BST Otp Zic2 glutamatergic subpopulation complete the list
   (@tbl-leads).

### How we got there

- **Units.** 12 animals per tissue (6 WildR, 6 SPF), amygdala and hypothalamus. Every Allen class,
  subclass and supertype with ≥ 25 nuclei in every animal gives 244 units.
- **Discover subpopulations.** popAlign compresses each unit into interpretable gene programs
  (oNMF) and fits Gaussian mixtures to find subpopulations. "None" is allowed. Each subpopulation
  is checked by bootstrap.
- **Test the microbiome.** For each animal we measure each subpopulation's *share* (composition)
  and its *position in program space* (state). WildR and SPF are compared by exact permutation of
  the 12 animals.
- **Guard against artefacts.**
  - normalisation matched to sequencing depth, with a depth flag and covariate;
  - a cross-lineage contamination screen, which found myelin RNA in hypothalamic neurons, relevant
    to every hypothalamic analysis;
  - gene annotation keyed on Ensembl IDs.

  A full audit trail is under [Code & Provenance](#code-provenance).

### What to do next

1. **Test the circuit hypothesis in space.** Score the shifted programs of the MeA / BST / medial
   hypothalamus leads in the seqFISH data, WildR vs SPF. That is an independent modality with
   anatomy attached.
2. **Connect the shifted programs to genes and to the relay analyses.** Test whether the genes
   in each moving program are enriched among MAST hits and D-SPIN responses of the same unit.
   Correlate per-animal state scores with the VR-1 / VR-2 relay scores.
3. **Harden the hypothalamic signal.** Decontaminate the hypothalamic counts (scCDC / CellBender),
   add a depth covariate to the state test, and re-test the enrichment.

## Background

D-SPIN gave us a regulatory-network view of how the microbiome perturbs supertype-level gene
programs. It assumes, though, that each supertype is a single population whose program
activities shift. Allen types are reference-defined. Within them, nuclei may occupy distinct
functional states that the taxonomy does not resolve, and a microbiome effect could act by
changing the **proportions** of those states rather than shifting a whole cell type.

PopAlign (Chen, Rivaud, Park, Tsou & Thomson, PNAS) models each sample as a Gaussian mixture over
interpretable oNMF gene programs. It aligns subpopulations across samples by Jeffrey's divergence
and quantifies abundance (Δw), mean-state (Δμ) and covariance (ΔΣ) changes. Running it at three
taxonomy depths asks three things. Do class-level subpopulations recover subclasses? Do subclass
subpopulations recover supertypes? And which states exist *within* a supertype that the
microbiome moves?

## Results

### The microbiome signal concentrates in one circuit {#sec-circuit}

[HEADLINE]{.eyebrow}

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-circuit
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("circuit_enrichment")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure A.**]{.fig-num} Share of units carrying a nominal microbiome state shift (any robust,
uncontaminated component with p < 0.05), for units from the medial amygdala, BST and medial
hypothalamic nuclei (orange) vs all other units (grey). Each unit counts once. Fisher's exact
test. The network is defined once, by Allen region names (MEA, BST, PVH, DMH, AHN, TMd, MPN, MPO,
VMH, SBPV), following the relay hypothesis of the VR analyses. It was defined once and not
iterated, but after the lead list had been seen, so treat this as a hypothesis-driven test rather
than a pre-registered one.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **`r sprintf("%.1f", E("all levels", "rate_in") / E("all levels", "rate_out"))`× the rate of state shifts.**
  `r pct(E("all levels", "rate_in"))` of network units vs `r pct(E("all levels", "rate_out"))` of all
  others (odds ratio `r ORf(E("all levels", "odds_ratio"))`,
  p = `r Pf(E("all levels", "p"))`). For the strongest shifts (p ≤ 0.0065) it is
  `r E("all levels", "in_group_hits", "strong")` vs `r E("all levels", "out_group_hits", "strong")`
  units (OR `r ORf(E("all levels", "odds_ratio", "strong"))`).
- **Not an artefact of unit size or test count.** Adjusting for number of subpopulations, nuclei,
  level and tissue gives OR `r ORf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "odds_ratio"))`
  (p = `r Pf(E("unit level, adjusted (n_comp, n_cells, level, tissue)", "p"))`). At component
  level it is OR `r ORf(E("component level, adjusted (n_cells, level, tissue)", "odds_ratio"))`.
- **Holds within each level, and points the same way in both tissues.** Subclass OR
  `r ORf(E("subclass only", "odds_ratio"))` (p = `r Pf(E("subclass only", "p"))`); supertype OR
  `r ORf(E("supertype only", "odds_ratio"))` (p = `r Pf(E("supertype only", "p"))`); hypothalamus
  OR `r ORf(E("HYP only", "odds_ratio"))` (p = `r Pf(E("HYP only", "p"))`); amygdala OR
  `r ORf(E("AMY only", "odds_ratio"))` (p = `r Pf(E("AMY only", "p"))`, fewer units).
- **It is anatomical, not a GABA effect.** Grouping by transmitter instead (GABA vs the rest) shows
  no enrichment. The network includes glutamatergic types (MEA-BST Otp Zic2, VMH Fezf1, PVH Otp).
:::

[Source: cell `cell-report-assets`](#cell-report-assets){.provenance} · tables:
[popAlign_circuit_enrichment.csv]{.path}, [popAlign_circuit_units.csv]{.path}
:::

### Composition is stable, even where DEGs are abundant {#sec-deg}

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-deg
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("deg_vs_composition")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure B.**]{.fig-num} Each point is a unit. The x-axis is the number of MAST DEGs (WildR vs SPF,
padj < 0.1) from the earlier differential-expression analysis. The y-axis is the evidence that the
unit's subpopulation mix differs between WildR and SPF (popAlign omnibus test). Dashed line:
p = 0.05.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **DEG-rich units keep their cell mix.** None of the `r if (!is.null(dvc)) nrow(dvc_top) else "—"`
  top-quartile DEG units shows a composition shift. Across all units, more DEGs go with slightly
  *less* compositional signal (Spearman ρ = `r if (!is.null(dvc)) sprintf("%.2f", deg_rho$estimate) else "—"`).
- **So the MAST DEGs are regulation within populations,** not a by-product of subpopulations
  growing or shrinking. That strengthens the interpretation of the DEG analysis.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-report-assets`](#cell-report-assets){.provenance} · table: [popAlign_deg_vs_composition.csv]{.path}
:::

### Priority follow-ups

[TOP HITS]{.eyebrow}

No microbiome effect survives FDR correction. With 6 vs 6 animals the smallest attainable exact
p is 2/924 ≈ 0.0022, which caps power. The leads below are therefore ranked by **internal
replication**, not by p alone. Each is a robust (bootstrap-stable), uncontaminated subpopulation
whose state or abundance differs between WildR and SPF at the animal level. Leads where the
*same* cell lineage is flagged by two separately fit models (its subclass **and** its supertype
run) come first. These models share nuclei and animals, so agreement shows robustness to
modelling rather than independent replication. Those leads are the best candidates for spatial
validation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-leads
#| echo: false
if (!is.null(leads)) {
  leads %>%
    mutate(
      Rank = row_number(),
      `Cell type` = glue("{tissue} · {lineage}"),
      Level = str_to_title(level),
      Effect = if_else(effect == "state shift", "State shift", glue("Abundance {direction}")),
      Evidence = if_else(effect == "state shift",
                         glue("p = {signif(p, 2)} (q = {signif(q, 2)})"),
                         glue("p = {signif(p, 2)}, {separation}/6 animals separated; depth-adj. p = {signif(p_abund_glm_depthadj, 2)}")),
      `Share of unit` = paste0(share_pct, "%"),
      Stability = sprintf("%.2f", stability),
      `What changes` = if_else(effect == "state shift",
                               glue("Program: {shifted_program_genes}"),
                               glue("{round(100 * mean_frac_SPF)}% → {round(100 * mean_frac_WildR)}% of nuclei (SPF → WildR)")),
      `Defining markers` = markers,
      Replicated = if_else(convergent, glue("★ {levels_hit}"), "—")
    ) %>%
    mutate(QC = if_else(depth_flag, "depth-associated", "clean")) %>%
    dplyr::select(Rank, `Cell type`, Level, Replicated, Effect, Evidence, `Share of unit`, Stability, QC, `What changes`, `Defining markers`) %>%
    kable(format = "html", escape = TRUE,
          caption = "Follow-up leads: robust, uncontaminated subpopulations (state p ≤ 0.0065, or abundance p < 0.05 with ≥5/6 animals separated and surviving depth adjustment). ★ = the same lineage is flagged in ≥2 separately fit units (nuclei overlap across levels). QC 'depth-associated' = the component differs from the rest of its unit by ≥26% in UMI depth; state tests carry no depth covariate, so treat those state leads with extra caution.")
}
```

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways: what to follow up first** (grouped by biology; ★ rows in the table above)

- **AMY MEA-BST Lhx6 Nr2e1 GABA. Strongest lead.** A state shift was flagged by both the
  subclass model (p = 0.0065) and the separately fit supertype 0355 model (p = 0.0043). Both components carry the same
  identity (*Reln, Cadps2, Zbtb20, Npas3, Dab1*) and are among the most stable in the dataset
  (stability 0.99). This is the MeA→BST relay studied in VR-1–VR-4. Next: test whether the shifted
  program tracks the VR relay scores per animal, and map the component in seqFISH.
- **HYP DMH Hmx2 GABA.** A state shift at the minimum attainable p in both the subclass
  (component 4) and supertype 0488 runs. The moving program contains *Erbb4* and *Htr2c* in both,
  so it is the same biology seen twice. The supertype component is depth-associated (≈25% lower
  UMI depth); the subclass hit is clean and carries the lead. A dorsomedial hypothalamic
  inhibitory population is a plausible microbiome-sensitive node (feeding / thermoregulation).
- **HYP MEA-BST Lhx6 Sp9, TMd-DMH Foxd2 and PVHd-DMH Lhx6 GABA.** Each has a large (46–56% of
  unit), stable, depth-clean component shifted at the minimum p. Together with DMH Hmx2, **all 5 state shifts
  at the minimum attainable p fall in the MeA–BST–medial-hypothalamus network**. They happen to be
  GABAergic, but the network enrichment (Fig. A) is not GABA-specific.
- **HYP PVH-SO-PVa Otp Glut (*Avp*). Neuroendocrine.** A state shift in the *Avp*-expressing
  component (p = 0.0043), affecting synaptic programs (*Nrg1, Kcnc2, Erbb4*). It is the most
  direct link to the stress / HPA axis among the leads.
- **AMY MEA-BST Otp Zic2 Glut. Best abundance lead.** The component grows from 32% to 43% of
  nuclei in WildR (5 of 6 animals separated). It survives depth adjustment (p = 0.002), and it
  sits in the same medial-amygdala relay as the MEA-BST Lhx6 Nr2e1 lead.
- **Caveat.** Individually these are leads, not findings (best q = 0.19). The stronger evidence is
  collective: shifts cluster in one circuit far more than chance allows (Fig. A).
:::

### How many subpopulations does each cell type contain?

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-overview
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("unit_overview")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 1.**]{.fig-num} Left: atlas GMM components per unit, chosen by held-out BIC from K = 1,
against unit size. The atlas is fit on up to 1,000 / 700 / 400 nuclei per animal (class /
subclass / supertype). Right: the fraction of 20 bootstraps (80% of the pool) that re-select
the same K.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **Substructure is the rule, not the exception.** Units contain a median of `r k_med[["class"]]`
  (class), `r k_med[["subclass"]]` (subclass) and `r k_med[["supertype"]]` (supertype)
  subpopulations. Only `r k1[["subclass"]]` subclass and `r k1[["supertype"]]` supertype units are
  homogeneous (K = 1).
- **The exact K is soft at class level.** Bootstraps re-select the same K in a median of
  `r pct(kagree[["class"]])` of refits for classes, against `r pct(kagree[["supertype"]])` for
  supertypes. Interpret class-level components through their per-component stability (Fig. 5),
  not through K.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-synthesis`](#cell-synthesis){.provenance}
:::

### Is subpopulation structure technical? Depth and contamination QC

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-depth
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("depth_qc")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 2.**]{.fig-num} Each component's median log10 UMI minus the rest of its unit. Real cell
types differ in RNA content (large cholinergic or projection neurons carry more), so depth
association alone is not grounds for exclusion. Components beyond ±0.1 log10 (≈26%) are flagged.
A flagged component's abundance shift counts only if it survives a quasi-binomial GLM with
per-animal median depth as a covariate. WildR and SPF differ by ≈5% in depth within tissue.
Sub-libraries are fully balanced.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **Depth tracks subpopulations mainly at coarse levels.** Component explains a median
  `r pct(eta[["class"]])` of per-nucleus depth variance in class units, falling to
  `r pct(eta[["supertype"]])` in supertypes. `r n_depth` components are depth-flagged. Every
  *abundance* lead survives the depth covariate; *state* leads in depth-associated components are
  marked in the leads table.
- **`r n_contam` components are cross-lineage contamination**, mostly myelin (*Plp1, Mbp, Mobp*)
  in hypothalamic neuronal units. They are labelled and excluded from all microbiome conclusions.
  None was a microbiome hit.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-synthesis`](#cell-synthesis){.provenance}
:::

### Which subpopulations change in abundance with the microbiome?

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-abundance
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("abundance_volcano")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 3.**]{.fig-num} Component abundance (Δw) tests on per-animal logit fractions, by exact
permutation over all 924 balanced relabelings of the 12 animals. In K = 2 units only the minority
component is tested. A unit-level omnibus (CLR fraction vectors) and a quasi-binomial GLM are in
the catalogue. BH correction is applied within each level. Dotted line: smallest attainable p.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **Abundance is essentially unchanged by the microbiome.** `r n_ab05` of `r n_ab` component tests
  (`r pct(n_ab05 / n_ab, 1)`) reach p < 0.05, *below* the 5% expected by chance. At the unit
  level, `r n_om05` of `r n_om` omnibus tests do (best q = `r round(minq_om, 2)`).
- **The few abundance leads are small, consistent shifts** (Fig. 4): 2–11 percentage points
  with 5/6 animals separated, not large population changes. The microbiome does not appear to
  reshape cell-type composition at this resolution.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-synthesis`](#cell-synthesis){.provenance}
:::

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}

show_fig("top_abundance_animals")
```

### Are subpopulations known Allen types or new cross-type states?

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-purity
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("purity_stability")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 5.**]{.fig-num} The x-axis is purity: the share of a component's nuclei carrying its most
common next-finer Allen label (subclass for class units, supertype for subclass units, cluster for
supertype units). The y-axis is clusterboot stability: the mean Jaccard overlap of its nuclei with
the best-matching component across 20 bootstraps that re-select K. Dotted line: 0.75 ("stable").
Crosses are depth-flagged.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **At coarse levels popAlign rediscovers the taxonomy.** Of the robust, clean components,
  `r kinds$"Allen-aligned subtype"[kinds$level == "class"]` / `r sum(rc$level == "class")` (class) and
  `r kinds$"Allen-aligned subtype"[kinds$level == "subclass"]` / `r sum(rc$level == "subclass")`
  (subclass) map onto a single finer Allen type. This independently validates both the method and
  the MapMyCells labels.
- **Within supertypes, new structure appears.** `r kinds$"cross-type state"[kinds$level == "supertype"]`
  of `r sum(rc$level == "supertype")` robust supertype components are *cross-type states* that cut
  across Allen clusters. These are the candidate functional states the taxonomy does not resolve.
  The strongest state leads, by contrast, are mostly known types whose expression state moves:
  3 of the 5 minimum-p leads are Allen-aligned (purity 0.86–1.0), and 2 are mixed or cross-type
  (0.64, 0.46).
:::

[Source: cell `cell-synthesis`](#cell-synthesis){.provenance}
:::

### Which subpopulations shift expression state?

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}
#| label: show-fig-state
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_fig("state_shift")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 6.**]{.fig-num} Within-component state test (Δμ). The statistic is the distance between the
WildR and SPF mean per-animal centroids in oNMF space, with each feature standardised by its
pooled within-group SD, tested by exact permutation. For K = 1 units this is a whole-population
shift.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **State is where the microbiome signal is.** `r n_st05` of `r n_st` state tests
  (`r pct(n_st05 / n_st, 1)`) reach p < 0.05, against 5% expected and against only
  `r pct(n_ab05 / n_ab, 1)` for abundance. That is a modest excess. Tests within a unit are not
  independent, so treat it as suggestive. Its strongest members sit in the MeA–BST–medial
  hypothalamus network (Fig. A). None survives FDR (best q = `r round(minq_st, 2)`).
- **Interpretation:** the microbiome is more likely to *tune the expression state* of specific
  inhibitory populations than to change how many cells of each kind there are.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-synthesis`](#cell-synthesis){.provenance}
:::

### Recurrent meta-programs across cell types

::: {.figure-card .fig-wide}
```{r}

show_fig("meta_programs_top")
```

::: {.fig-caption}
[**Figure 7.**]{.fig-num} The 20 largest meta-programs, each present in ≥ 4 units (click to
enlarge). Specificity-ranked marker sets (top 50 by AUC ≥ 0.6) are linked across all units by
Jaccard ≥ 0.15 and clustered with Leiden. Each tile marks a unit (column) containing a component
of that meta-program (row), coloured by Allen level. Tissues are shown separately. The table below
lists every meta-program present in ≥ 4 units; all `r if (!is.null(mp_sum)) nrow(mp_sum) else "—"`
are in [popAlign_meta_program_summary.csv]{.path}.
:::

::: {.takeaways}
**Key takeaways**

- **The two largest "programs" are contamination, not biology.** MP56 and MP46 (*Plp1, Mbp, Mobp*)
  span the most units, but most of their members are flagged myelin contamination in hypothalamic
  neurons. They are ambient RNA / doublet signatures and should be ignored as states.
- **Genuine shared programs are lineage-restricted.** Most real meta-programs stay inside one
  tissue and one family of related types: MP16 across amygdalar cortical-type GABA interneurons
  (Vip, Sst, Pvalb, Lamp5, Sncg); MP2 and MP3 (*Bdnf, Mapk4*, an activity-linked program) across
  amygdalar glutamatergic types (LA-BLA-BMA-PA, L2/3 IT PIR-ENTl, MEA). Programs that cut across
  lineages are rare.
:::

[Source: cell `cell-report-assets`](#cell-report-assets){.provenance}
:::

```{r}
  n_show <- 10

```

`robust` requires substructure (K > 1), stability ≥ 0.75, weight ≥ 2% and ≥10 markers. A microbiome
hit is reported only for robust, uncontaminated components; depth-flagged components must also
pass the depth-adjusted GLM. *Score* adds robust and clean (1) + GO-annotated (1) + ≥25 markers
(0.5) + meta-program member (0.5) + D-SPIN overlap (0.5). Full table:
[tables/popAlign/snRNASeq/run_2026-10-04_synth-2026-10-05/popAlign_subpopulation_catalog.csv]{.path}.

| Step | What | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Manifest | Unit inclusion at class / subclass / supertype from `cell_meta_keep_cell.csv` | direct (seconds) |
| 2. Export | Raw-UMI 10x mtx per unit; gene QC (≥10 nuclei; drop mt-/Rpl/Rps). Inputs shared across runs; only missing units exported | SLURM, 400 GB |
| 3. popAlign | β = unit median UMI → variable genes → oNMF (*m* searched widely) → per-animal GMMs (10 replicates) → atlas GMM (K from 1, held-out BIC) → clusterboot stability (K re-selected per bootstrap) → conservative JD alignment → native Δ / LLR → specificity-ranked markers | SLURM array, 244 tasks |
| 4. Synthesis | Unit omnibus + component abundance tests (exact permutation, quasi-binomial secondary), state shift, depth QC, Allen purity, GO, D-SPIN / MAST overlap, meta-programs, class→subclass→supertype maps, catalogue | SLURM, 1 job |

Manifest: [data/interim/popalign/snRNASeq/manifest_2026-10-04.csv]{.path} · results:
[data/interim/popalign/snRNASeq/results_2026-10-04/&lt;level&gt;/&lt;tissue&gt;__&lt;label&gt;/]{.path}

## Synthesis & Discussion

[SYNTHESIS]{.eyebrow}

**The question.** Does a wild-type microbiome change *which* cells make up the amygdala and
hypothalamus, or *how* those cells are tuned? And if so, where?

**What we learned.**

- *Composition is resilient.* Down to sub-supertype resolution, the relative sizes of
  subpopulations are indistinguishable between WildR and SPF animals. This is a substantive
  negative result: whatever the microbiome does to these brain regions, it does not reshape their
  cellular make-up at a scale 12 animals can detect. It also tells us something about the earlier
  differential-expression results. The cell types with the most DEGs are exactly as stable in
  composition as the rest (Fig. B), so those DEGs report regulation within cells, not changes in
  the cell mix.
- *The signal is in cell state, and it has an address.* State shifts are only modestly more common
  than chance overall (`r pct(n_st05 / n_st, 1)` vs 5%). They are far from randomly placed,
  though: they occur at about 2.6× the background rate (odds ratio about 4) in the medial
  amygdala → BST → medial hypothalamus network (Fig. A), which holds 11 of the 13 strongest. With
  n = 6 per group, a hypothesis-driven enrichment across many units is a more appropriate test
  than per-unit FDR, and it is the strongest statistical result in this analysis.
- *The taxonomy is real, and has more below it.* popAlign, which never sees the Allen labels,
  recovers them at class and subclass level. Within supertypes, about a third of robust
  subpopulations are states that cut across clusters. The method therefore resolves biology finer
  than the reference; for this question, that finer structure did not turn out to be where the
  microbiome acts.

**Why the circuit result is credible.**

1. It aggregates many sub-threshold units instead of relying on one, which suits a 6-vs-6 design.
2. It survives adjustment for the obvious confounds: unit size, number of subpopulations, level
   and tissue.
3. It is anatomical rather than defined by cell class. A GABA-vs-rest grouping shows nothing.
4. The network is motivated by the earlier VR relay analyses, not by searching for the best
   grouping.
5. The programs that move are coherent: synaptic receptor and adhesion genes, with no
   immediate-early activity genes.

**Why it is not yet proof.**

1. Subclass and supertype units share nuclei and animals, so the per-level results are two views
   of one dataset, not two replications.
2. The network is defined by Allen region names. That is principled, but these regions are
   heterogeneous, and the set (MEA, BST, PVH, DMH, AHN, TMd, MPN, MPO, VMH, SBPV) is one reasonable
   choice among several.
3. The state test has no depth covariate, and three state leads sit in depth-associated components.
4. Hypothalamic counts carry myelin ambient RNA or doublets. They are flagged, not removed.
5. The network grouping was defined after the leads had been seen (one definition, a GABA grouping
   tested first and found null). It is hypothesis-driven, not pre-registered. A confirmatory test
   needs new data.
6. Everything rests on one cohort of 12 animals.

**What it could mean.** This network is the main route by which chemosensory social cues, including
vomeronasal input, reach neuroendocrine and behavioural output: social, defensive and
reproductive behaviour, and stress via PVH *Avp* neurons. The microbiome is widely reported to
influence social behaviour and stress-axis reactivity. Two non-exclusive routes would explain a
microbiome effect focused here:

- an altered **chemosensory environment**: microbially shaped odours and pheromonal cues read
  through the vomeronasal relay, which is the hypothesis behind VR-1–VR-4;
- **direct signalling** to this hormone- and metabolite-sensitive circuit.

Either way, the data point to retuning of synaptic receptor and adhesion programs, a lasting change
in how these cells process input, rather than a change in how active they were when sampled.

**How it fits with the other analyses.**

- *VR relay notebooks:* the convergence is anatomical; popAlign independently highlights the same
  MeA–BST relay populations.
- *MAST and D-SPIN:* at the gene level the overlap is weak. Lead identity markers rarely contain
  MAST hits (12% vs 25% overall), and overlap with D-SPIN programs is weak (Jaccard ≤ 0.10). Part
  of this is expected, because markers describe identity, not change. The decisive comparison,
  between shifted-program genes and MAST / D-SPIN, has not been done yet.

**Bottom line.** The microbiome does not rebuild these brain regions; at most it retunes them, and
the retuning points to one circuit. That is a specific, falsifiable hypothesis, and the next
experiments test it directly: seqFISH within the network, and gene-level links to MAST, D-SPIN
and the VR scores.

## Next Steps

- We modelled 244 units at three Allen levels and tested every subpopulation at the animal level.
  Composition is unchanged. State shifts concentrate in the MeA → BST → medial hypothalamus network
  (Fig. A), which is now the hypothesis to test.
- **Validate the leads spatially (highest priority).** Score the identity markers and shifted
  programs of the ★ leads (MEA-BST Lhx6 Nr2e1, DMH Hmx2) and the medial-hypothalamic Lhx6 / Foxd2
  GABA leads on the seqFISH data, to locate them anatomically and test the WildR vs SPF difference in
  an independent modality.
- **Compare shifted programs, not markers, with MAST / D-SPIN.** For each lead, test whether the
  genes in the moving oNMF program are enriched among MAST hits and D-SPIN-responsive programs of
  the same unit. That is the gene-level bridge this report does not yet make.
- **Link to the VR relay analyses.** Correlate per-animal component state scores of the MeA–BST
  leads with the VR-1 input/output coupling scores and VR-2 program identity scores.
- **Firm up the state test.** Add a per-animal depth covariate to the state shift test, and re-run
  hypothalamic units on decontaminated counts (scCDC / CellBender) to remove the myelin signal.
- **Sensitivity.** Re-run the leads with `criteria='aic'` and leave-one-animal-out atlases, to
  confirm no single animal or model-selection choice drives them.
- **Cell-cap sensitivity.** Eight units were capped at 2,500 nuclei per animal (uniform random
  within animal, seed 42; 113,769 nuclei not exported):
  - *class:* AMY 01 IT-ET Glut (34% of nuclei kept), AMY 11 CNU-HYa GABA (98%), HYP 12 HY GABA (61%),
    HYP 14 HY Glut (63%), HYP 31 OPC-Oligo (79%);
  - *subclass:* AMY 009 L2/3 IT PIR-ENTl Glut (83%), HYP 327 Oligo NN (89%);
  - *supertype:* HYP 1184 MOL NN_4 (91%).

  The atlas GMM is fit on at most 1,000 / 700 / 400 nuclei per animal anyway, so the cap mainly
  limits how many nuclei are assigned when per-animal fractions are estimated. It does not limit
  model fitting. Uniform within-animal sampling keeps those fractions unbiased, but states below
  ~1% of a unit get few nuclei. Re-run these eight at 5,000 per animal (AMY 01 IT-ET Glut alone
  loses two-thirds of its nuclei).

# Code & Provenance {.code-appendix}

All heavy computation runs in scripts and is submitted to SLURM. **None of the chunks below run
on render**: they are gated on `run_analysis` (set in `setup-display`). To reproduce, run them in
order with `run_analysis <- TRUE`, or run the commands by hand. Logs and job IDs are in
[.cluster_runs/popalign/]{.path} (`submissions.log`).

### Run history

| Run | Date | Units | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `results/` (manifest.csv) | 2026-10-02 | 160 (class, supertype) | **Superseded.** Kept on disk for comparison; do not interpret. |
| `results_2026-10-04/`, synthesis `run_2026-10-04/` | 2026-10-05 | 244 (class, subclass, supertype) | Superseded synthesis: GO keyed on ambiguous symbols; no contamination flag |
| `results_2026-10-04/`, synthesis `run_2026-10-04_synth-2026-10-05/` | 2026-10-05 | 244 | **Current** |

**Re-synthesis 2026-10-05 (popAlign runs unchanged).**

1. **Gene identity.** Seurat row names carry a genome tag plus de-duplication suffixes
   (`Arhgap26-GRCm39-1`). 288 features share a `gene_name` with another Ensembl ID; for example,
   `Arhgap26-GRCm39-1` is ENSMUSG00000118193, a lncRNA distinct from protein-coding *Arhgap26*.
   Symbol-based GO therefore conflated distinct genes and dropped suffixed ones. The RNA
   `meta.features` (`gene_id`, `gene_name`, `gene_type`) was exported to
   [data/interim/seurat/snRNASeq/seurat_gene_metadata_2026-10-05.csv]{.path}. All 32,684 genes
   used across the 244 units map 1:1 to Ensembl IDs. GO now runs on `gene_id`
   (`keyType = "ENSEMBL"`, with each unit's own background), and markers are displayed by
   `gene_name`.
2. **Cross-lineage contamination flag.** About 6% of neuronal components (46 / 750) carry
   another lineage's genes among their top markers, almost all myelin in hypothalamic units (43 of 44
   myelin flags in neuronal units), and an OPC subclass component had a neuronal signature
   (*Snhg11, Rian, Syt1, Rbfox3*). This is likely ambient RNA or doublets rather than states. A
   component is flagged when ≥2 canonical genes of a lineage the unit does not belong to are in
   its top-50 markers. The lineage sets are oligodendrocyte, OPC, astrocyte, microglia,
   endothelial and neuronal; the unit's own lineage comes from its Allen name. Flagged components
   are kept but excluded from microbiome conclusions and the interpretability score. GO on
   flagged myelin components returns "myelination", which independently supports the flag.

**Why the 2026-10-02 run was superseded.** An audit against the paper and the official tutorial
(`tutorials/PopAlign_Tutorial_v1.ipynb`), and against that run's own outputs, found:

1. **Forced splits.** The atlas K search started at 2 (supertype) and 3 (class). 127/139 supertype
   and 9/21 class units sat at that floor, and when K = 1 was allowed, 18 of 40 sampled supertype
   units preferred it. *Fix: K from 1.*
2. **Uninformative stability.** Bootstraps reused the same K and scored mutual-best JD matches,
   which is near-automatic for K = 2 (mean 0.98). *Fix: clusterboot. K is re-selected in each
   bootstrap, and each component is scored by the Jaccard overlap of its nuclei; ≥ 0.75 = stable.*
3. **β too low.** The paper and tutorial set β = 1000 because it is *"roughly the median number
   of total transcript counts in a cell"*. Our nuclei carry about 7–30k (neurons) and 1.3–6k
   (glia) UMIs, so β = 1000 made the log transform nearly linear. *Fix: β = unit median UMI per
   nucleus (median 12.6k across units, IQR 9.7–14.9k).*
4. **oNMF *m* hit the search bound.** The supertype median of 12 was the maximum searched, and
   class units reached 16, also the maximum. *Fix: m ∈ 6–24 / 4–22 / 4–20 (class / subclass /
   supertype); hitting a bound is now recorded per unit.*
5. **Depth.** WildR vs SPF depth differs by about 5% within tissue, and some class components
   tracked depth (up to 57% of log-UMI variance). *Fix: per-nucleus depth is recorded and
   components with |Δ log10 UMI| ≥ 0.1 are flagged. A flagged component's abundance shift must
   survive a depth-adjusted quasi-binomial GLM (per-animal median depth covariate), and any hit
   requires a robust component.*
6. **Markers favoured broadly expressed long genes.** 375/396 components fell into 14 generic
   meta-programs. *Fix: candidates need log2FC ≥ 0.5, Δ expressing fraction ≥ 0.05 and
   pct ≥ 0.10, ranked by AUC (≥ 0.6).*
7. **Redundant K = 2 tests.** *Fix: only the minority component is tested; a unit omnibus test is
   added.*
8. **Power ceiling not stated.** *Fix: the minimum attainable p is shown; complete separation and
   effect size are reported; a quasi-binomial GLM gives continuous p as a secondary test.*
9. **Atlas pools equalised to the smallest animal** (312–582 nuclei for 12-D full-covariance
   GMMs). *Fix: cap each animal (1,000 / 700 / 400) without equalising; the 6 vs 6 design keeps
   groups balanced.*

The audit also found that popAlign's `JeffreyDiv` returns **log10** JD (negative = JD < 1). The
synthesis now handles that scale correctly.

**Checked and unchanged.**

- *Inputs:* raw integer counts; barcode and metadata order verified; mt-/Rpl/Rps removed upstream,
  because popAlign's prefix filter is human-only and `load_genes` upper-cases symbols (original
  case is restored on output).
- *Inclusion and cap:* ≥25 nuclei per animal; 2,500 per-animal cap; balanced sub-libraries.
- *Gene filter:* supra-Poisson CV filter with offset 1.0 (the tutorial uses 1.3; the paper does
  not specify), unaffected by β.
- *Model fitting:* oNMF training cells and `choose_featureset(alpha=3, multiplier=3)` as in the
  tutorial; held-out BIC; covariance regularisation = popAlign default (top program variance /
  100).
- *Reproducibility:* popAlign's per-animal GMMs reseed from entropy (`np.random.seed()` inside
  `build_single_GMM`), so the native alignment and Δ outputs are not bit-reproducible. The
  primary atlas analysis is seeded.

**Environment.** popAlign is the lab fork `jboktor/popalign` at commit `d9a0c1a`, cloned at
[/resnick/groups/mthomson/jboktor/spatial_genomics/popalign]{.path}. Jobs put it on `PYTHONPATH`
in a dedicated `popalign` conda env (Python 3.9). The runner works around three
environment issues without editing popAlign:

- forked Pool workers hang, so the runner uses a forkserver Pool;
- matplotlib ≥ 3.9 renamed `legendHandles`, so the runner adds an alias;
- `rank()` fails on animals below `mincells`, so the runner sets `mincells` below the smallest
  animal.

R steps use the `spatialomics` env.


```{r}
#| label: cell-submit
#| eval: !expr run_analysis
# Steps 2–4 — chained SLURM submission: export (missing inputs only) → popAlign array → synthesis
sb <- function(cmd) {
  out <- system(glue("cd {wkdir} && {cmd}"), intern = TRUE)
  message(out); sub(".*?([0-9]+).*", "\\1", tail(out, 1))
}
man_rel <- glue("data/interim/popalign/snRNASeq/manifest_{run_tag}.csv")
n_task <- nrow(read_csv(file.path(wkdir, man_rel), show_col_types = FALSE))
j_export <- sb(glue("sbatch --parsable notebooks/shell_scripts/run_popalign_export_sn.sh {run_tag}"))
j_array <- sb(glue("sbatch --parsable --array=0-{n_task - 1}%40 --dependency=afterok:{j_export} ",
                   "notebooks/shell_scripts/run_popalign_array_sn.sh {man_rel}"))
j_synth <- sb(glue("sbatch --parsable --dependency=afterany:{j_array} ",
                   "notebooks/shell_scripts/run_popalign_synthesis_sn.sh --run-tag {run_tag}"))
tibble(step = c("export", "popalign_array", "synthesis"), job_id = c(j_export, j_array, j_synth))
# Run 2026-10-04 as actually submitted: see .cluster_runs/popalign/submissions.log
```
